figures.caption: Figure 2 | Consequences of 'who's on first' in DNA-damage recognition. Recognition of DNA damage is required for repair, either by direct reversal or by repair pathways. The schematic presents only eukaryotic proteins. Direct repair of UV photoproducts and alkylation damage is catalysed by photolyases, alkyltransferases and dioxygenases. DNA glycosylases (TABLE 1) recognize damage that is to be processed by base excision repair (BER); XPC/HR23B, XPE and their orthologues identify damage destined for nucleotide excision repair (NER); and the MutS complexes target DNA modifications for mismatch repair (MMR). The signal for transcriptioncoupled repair (TCR) is generated by an RNA polymerase (RNAP) that is arrested at a site of DNA damage in the transcribed strand. Other cellular factors (represented by a yellow octagon) that interact with DNA damage could have at least three consequences: facilitation of repair (FIG. 3); interference with repair (FIG. 4); or redirection of DNA-damage processing (FIG. 5). The listing of proteins under one or more of these consequences is based on their binding to damaged DNA (TABLE 2), and either their effects in vitro on the repair of a particular form of damage or their contribution to a cellular phenotype in response to a damaging agent.

figures.caption: Figure 3 | Consequence 1 - facilitation of repair. The cellular factors listed (represented by a green octagon) have favourable effects on the repair of some forms of DNA damage and/or cellular sensitivity to certain DNA-damaging agents. When bound at a site of damage, these factors might function as 'antennae' to alert repair-recognition factors that damage is present. The factors could dissociate and allow access to the lesion or form a complex with the repairrecognition factors to signal for damage repair. In the case of transcription-coupled repair (TCR), the cellular factors might arrest RNA polymerase (RNAP) at a site of damage that would not otherwise trigger TCR by polymerase arrest. αSpIIΣ*, human α-spectrin II; ATR, ataxiatelangiectasia mutated (ATM)-related protein; HMG, high-mobility group; Nhp, HMG1-like transcriptional regulator of RNA polymerase II and III; YB-1, Y-box-binding protein-1.

figures.caption: Figure 4 | Consequence 2 - interference with repair. The cellular factors listed (represented by a red octagon) have negative effects on the repair of some forms of DNA damage and/or cellular sensitivity to certain DNA-damaging agents. When bound at a site of damage, these factors might obscure lesions from repair-recognition factors. When present at damage on the transcribed strand, the factors might block the RNA polymerase (RNAP), but prevent transcription-coupled repair (TCR) signalling. Alternatively, they might allow RNAP to bypass the lesion. If the factor is a topoisomerase, the translocating polymerase can rupture the covalent topoisomerase-DNA complex and create strand breaks 125 . A result of factor interference with repair could be a compounding of DNA damage, which might lead to errant transcripts, genetic instability, mutagenesis and, possibly, cell death. HMG, high-mobility group; Ixr1, intrastrand cross-link recognition protein; mtTFA, mitochondrial transcription factor; TBP, TATA-binding protein; Top1, topoisomerase I; tsHMG, mouse testis specific HMG.

figures.caption: Figure 5 | Consequence 3 - redirection of damage processing. Cellular factors (represented by a brown octagon) might also redirect the processing of DNA damage, which could allow for the repair of one type of damage by numerous pathways or control the timing of DNA repair and cell-cycle progression. First, the factor could alter DNA-damage signalling by blocking damage recognition by the repair enzymes of one pathway and promoting damage recognition by other repair pathways, or by the apoptosis mechanism, as is the case with O 6 -alkylguanine alkyltransferase (AGT) blocking nucleotide excision repair (NER) of alkylation damage 24 . Second, as mentioned in FIG. 3, a factor might block RNA polymerase at a lesion that is not normally subject to transcription-coupled repair. The scenario involving topoisomerases in FIG. 4 could also convert base damage to strand breaks that are then processed by DNA-break repair mechanisms 125 . Third, the factor could interact with the downstream proteins of a pathway, bypassing the need for the repair-recognition protein. An example of this is the interaction of MutS homologue 2 (MSH2) with NER proteins in yeast 70 .
